messages.subject: Re: contrast coding and lrm
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jorrig,

before I can answer your question, I need a little bit more information:

We created a logistic regression model to investigate the influence of
> different factors on Dutch word order variation. To avoid collinearity and
> to increase interpretability of the effects, we decided to center the
> predictors. For one predictor with two levels and one ordinal (5 point
> scale) predictor, we did this by subtracting the mean; for a third predictor
> with three levels, we used contrast coding. The levels of the latter
> predictor (called PP_TYPE_3) were coded as follows:
>
>     [,1] [,2]
> abs     1    0
> loc     0    1
> temp   -1   -1
>

is this the output of contrasts(dataframe$PP_TYPE_3)?

are you sure you applied the contrast specification, e.g.
contrasts(dataframe$PP_TYPE_3) = contr.sum(3), immediately before the
analysis and AFTER any other subsetting of the data.frame? Subsetting the
dataframe will destroy contrast specification, as I recall.


> The model summary gives us the following:
>
>                  Coef     S.E.    Wald Z P
> Intercept         -0.26760 0.10303 -2.60  0.0094
> cDEF3S            -0.27503 0.06216 -4.42  0.0000
> cANIM2_S          -0.17869 0.18324 -0.98  0.3295
> PP_TYPE_3=loc      0.60699 0.13471  4.51  0.0000
> PP_TYPE_3=temp     0.08269 0.12773  0.65  0.5174
> cDEF3S * cANIM2_S -0.38080 0.12298 -3.10  0.0020
>
> The names suggest that the model gives the estimates for the levels 'loc'
> and 'temp', taking 'abs' as reference level. But this is not what we want,
> is it? Shouldn't the model have taken the columns of the contrast matrix as
> the recoded factors?
>

yes, I am surprised by the output. if you just specified contrasts as I
describe above, I believe the predictors for PP_TYPE_3 should look like

PP_TYPE31 ...
PP_TYPE32 ...

where the 1 and 2 refer to the contrasts.

>
> We are also a bit confused about the correct interpretation of the
> estimates of the three-level predictor. Do these represent the difference
> between one level and the intercept (=the grand mean), or between one level
> and the mean of the other levels of that predictor?
>
> As a side question: is it correct to center the ordinal predictor the way
> we did?
>

which predictor do you mean by the ordinal one? you can center binary
predictors (whether you interpret the between-group difference as ordinal or
non-ordinal is up to you). Note though that coding (and centering) has
consequences for the random effect correlations (the random covariances; cf.
some of Harald Baayen's recent tutorials).

Florian


>
>
> Thanks for your help!
>
> Best,
> Jorrig Vogels
> Geertje van Bergen
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Claire,

sorry for the delayed response. I received your email while I was giving a
workshop in Groningen. Thanks for sending the data set and the script. I
still have some questions:

In response to all your comments...
> 1-
> Both script and data excerpt are attached.
> My dataset is a list of French sentences with RCs attached to NP1 or
> NP2 in a 'NP1 of NP2' compound. My binomial DV is the attachment to
> one of the possible antecedents.The model evaluates the factors
> guiding this attachment. The initial model contains all the variables
> of interest as main predictors, and interactions of interest, between
> one predictor and the others.
> Binomial variables are dummy coded and centered, the other variables
> are ordered then centered.
>

Do you mean that binary variables were dummy coded and centered, and that
continuous variables were centered? I am not sure what you mean by "ordered
and then centered". From the output you presented below, it seems to me that
you translated n-ary factorial contrasts into numeric values and then
centered that variable? That would lead to results that would be very hard
to interpret or not interpretable at all. If you are assuming that the
levels of e.g. definiteness are ordered, then I recommend that you use
Helmert coding or polynomial coding to test this hypothesis.

Are all factors in your model part of your design (i.e. are they balanced)?
If not, there's a whole set of additional issues and you should probably
conduct some sort of bootstrap over your model or at least evaluate the
quality of your model (see the Jaeger and Kuperman 2009 tutorial on the HLP
lab blog).

What are the questions you want to ask/the hypotheses you want to test?

Are the cell means of your factorial design for the proportions of the
outcome (E.g. attachment to N1) within 30-70%? If so, I would highly
recommend to you that use ANOVA with a empirical logit transform, following
the description given on Dale Barr's blog/website (he's doing eye-tracking
analysis, but empirical logits can be used for any outcome that is expressed
as proportion). Until have read more about mixed models, it will be
unnecessarily complicated to conduct the analyses required by the reviewers.
But see below.


These predictors are:
> - type of relativiser (qui, lequel). This is the predictor for which
> we test the interaction with the other predictors
> - animacy of NP1 (animate, inanimate)
> - animacy of NP2 (animate, inanimate)
> - modifier for NP1 (modifier, no modifier)
> - modifier for NP2 (modifier, no modifier)
> - syntactic function of NP1 in the main clause (subject, direct object,
> other)
> - definiteness of NP1 (Definite, Other, ProperName, Indefinite)
> - definiteness of NP2 (Definite, Other, ProperName, Indefinite)
>

could you provide the variable name for each predictor, so that one can
easily map the predictor to the output of the model you're providing below?

>
> The random term is sentence number.
>

I assume you mean that you had a random by-sentence intercept?



> 3-
> Here is my final model:
> > summary(model4.Attachment)
> Generalized linear mixed model fit by the Laplace approximation
> Formula: corpus$Attachment ~ corpus.cRel + corpus.cN1Animacy +
> corpus.cN2Animacy +      corpus.cN1Adjective + corpus.cN2Adjective +
> corpus.N1FunctionNA +      corpus.N1Definiteness +
> corpus.N2Definiteness + (1 | corpus$Corpustext) +
> corpus.cRel:corpus.cN1Animacy + corpus.cRel:corpus.cN2Animacy +
> corpus.cRel:corpus.N1FunctionNA
>    Data: corpus
>   AIC  BIC logLik deviance
>  1488 1586   -725     1450
> Random effects:
>  Groups            Name        Variance   Std.Dev.
>  corpus$Corpustext (Intercept) 1.9668e-09 4.4349e-05
> Number of obs: 1277, groups: corpus$Corpustext, 1117
>
> Fixed effects:
>                                  Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
> (Intercept)                      -0.31162    0.20410  -1.527  0.12681
> corpus.cRel                       3.25745    1.12139   2.905  0.00367 **
> corpus.cN1Animacy                 1.25938    0.16465   7.649 2.02e-14 ***
> corpus.cN2Animacy                -1.29455    0.14201  -9.116  < 2e-16 ***
> corpus.cN1Adjective               0.48364    0.14911   3.244  0.00118 **
> corpus.cN2Adjective              -0.65529    0.14503  -4.518 6.23e-06 ***
> corpus.N1FunctionNA2              0.65437    0.22362   2.926  0.00343 **
> corpus.N1FunctionNA3              0.56949    0.20890   2.726  0.00641 **
> corpus.N1Definiteness2           -0.83826    0.48813  -1.717  0.08593 .
> corpus.N1Definiteness3            0.42787    1.66453   0.257  0.79714
> corpus.N1Definiteness4            0.30884    0.15162   2.037  0.04166 *
> corpus.N2Definiteness2            1.33948    0.29053   4.611 4.02e-06 ***
> corpus.N2Definiteness3            0.08785    0.17777   0.494  0.62119
> corpus.N2Definiteness4           -0.39484    0.17830  -2.215  0.02679 *
> corpus.cRel:corpus.cN1Animacy    -1.28508    0.45951  -2.797  0.00516 **
> corpus.cRel:corpus.cN2Animacy    -0.39892    0.43056  -0.927  0.35417
> corpus.cRel:corpus.N1FunctionNA2 -2.78317    1.16899  -2.381  0.01727 *
> corpus.cRel:corpus.N1FunctionNA3 -3.00577    1.14153  -2.633  0.00846 **
> ---
> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
>
> 4-
> Because cRel and N1FunctionNA are highly correlated, I residualise
> them, removing collinearity. Correlation between cRel and cN1Animacy
> is more than acceptable so no residualisation is necessary.
>

Beware that it matters what you residualize against what. This will affect
the interpretation of the coefficient associated with the two predictors.

>
> 5-
> Reviewers are asking for Anova-like simple effect analysis for my two
> significant interactions (cRel:cN1Animacy, and cRel:N1FunctionNA). Are
> they higher order or 2 way interactions, I'd say the latter but cannot
> find a definition for the earlier.
> I tried to recode the variables in the end of my script, but I am not
> sure I am doing the right thing.
>

Now, if you insist on using mixed models, and you fix the coding of your
n-ary predictors as described above (if you didn't already do that), then
you're indeed dealing with two-way interactions. That's good news since it
makes testing for simple effects a lot easier. You can specify the relevant
terms by entering the two-way interaction into the model while at the same
time removing the main effects. E.g. instead of

corpus.cRel * corpus.cN1Animacy


you would enter into the model

corpus.cRel:corpus.cN1Animacy - corpus.cN1Animacy


The first specification (corpus.cRel*corpus.cN1Animacy) gave you what you
reported below: two main effects and an interaction. The second
specification (corpus.cRel:corpus.cN1Animacy - corpus.cN1Animacy) should
give you the effect of corpus.cRel*qui*, but remove the main effect
of cN1Animacy, instead providing two simple effects, something
like: corpus.cRel*qui*:corpus.cN1Animacy*Inanimate* and corpus.cRel*lequel*
:corpus.cN1Animacy*Inanimate*. That is, with this particular specification
you would get two parameters that describe the effect of Animacy for the two
different levels of corpus.cRel, which is what a simple effect analysis is
supposed to do.

The output will look somewhat different since you will be using contrast
coding and what I described in the preceding paragraph is based on the
assumption that you're using dummy coding.

HTH,

Florian

>
> Many, many thanks,
>
> Claire Delle Luche
>

To answer your questions:

temp   -1   -1

is this the output of contrasts(dataframe$PP_TYPE_3)?


Yes, except for the labels of the levels, which we obtain by just calling the predictor variable after applying the contrasts.



are you sure you applied the contrast specification, e.g. contrasts(dataframe$PP_TYPE_3) = contr.sum(3), immediately before the analysis and AFTER any other subsetting of the data.frame? Subsetting the dataframe will destroy contrast specification, as I recall.


We did not do any subsetting after specification of the contrasts, which we did exactly as you say.


The model summary gives us the following:

                 Coef     S.E.    Wald Z P
Intercept         -0.26760 0.10303 -2.60  0.0094
cDEF3S            -0.27503 0.06216 -4.42  0.0000
cANIM2_S          -0.17869 0.18324 -0.98  0.3295
PP_TYPE_3=loc      0.60699 0.13471  4.51  0.0000
PP_TYPE_3=temp     0.08269 0.12773  0.65  0.5174
cDEF3S * cANIM2_S -0.38080 0.12298 -3.10  0.0020

The names suggest that the model gives the estimates for the levels 'loc' and 'temp', taking 'abs' as reference level. But this is not what we want, is it? Shouldn't the model have taken the columns of the contrast matrix as the recoded factors?

yes, I am surprised by the output. if you just specified contrasts as I describe above, I believe the predictors for PP_TYPE_3 should look like

PP_TYPE31 ...
PP_TYPE32 ...

where the 1 and 2 refer to the contrasts.


Yes, that was also what I got when I was working with a different dataset and used lmer. I did the contrast specification in exactly the same way. So that suggests that it has something to do with the type of model.


We are also a bit confused about the correct interpretation of the estimates of the three-level predictor. Do these represent the difference between one level and the intercept (=the grand mean), or between one level and the mean of the other levels of that predictor?

As a side question: is it correct to center the ordinal predictor the way we did?

which predictor do you mean by the ordinal one? you can center binary predictors (whether you interpret the between-group difference as ordinal or non-ordinal is up to you). Note though that coding (and centering) has consequences for the random effect correlations (the random covariances; cf. some of Harald Baayen's recent tutorials).


DEF3S is the ordinal predictor. It specifies 5 levels of definiteness, from highly non-specific to highly specific. So there is an inherent order, but the distances between the levels are not necessarily equal. Maureen suggested that we could use Helmert coding or Forward/Backward difference coding. That seems to work out well.

Jorrig




Florian



Thanks for your help!

Best,
Jorrig Vogels
Geertje van Bergen

messages.subject: Advice needed on reading large text file in R
messages.subject_clean: Advice needed on reading large text file in R
messages.body_plain:
I have a text file encoded in CSV format that I plan to run a series of
linguistic analysis upon using R. My first thought is to use the read.csv
function to get the data into R. But suspect that this might be naive as the
file itself contains over 250,000 records and occupies over 1.5Gbytes of
disk space in its raw form. Each record has a large text field that extends
of multiple lines of the file; in some records this is equivalent to a few
paragraphs in other the text would run to pages. There is a second multiline
text field but this is much shorter --- maybe 20 different phrases. There
appear to escaped quotes throughout; though with a file this size verifying
this is difficult and some text editor crash trying to read it all in. I am
therefore dubious that read.csv is the right mechanism and seeking a better
method.

I am open to suggestions for input method and even segmentation if
necessary, provided segmentation does not prevent analysis of the entire
data. Would access to the records by R be any quicker if I pre-processed the
file into some relational/object database prior to analysis?

I will note in passing I did not collect the original data neither did I
decide to use CSV. This is the format in which the file was given to me for
the purposes of my study. CSV is the worst possible format for the
originator to have used for such a large collection of text.

Regards, Trevor.

<>< Re: deemed!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Trevor,

My guess is that you'll want to do something with that data once you
read it in, and that may be an even trickier challenge. Fortunately,
there have been a number of advances in working with "Big Data" (i.e.,
big enough that the size itself imposes challenges), and the company
Revolution Analytics has put some packages together, among other
people. Here's a blog post from just yesterday that has some slides
that might be helpful for you.

http://blog.revolutionanalytics.com/2011/09/analyzing-big-data-in-r-two-presentations-from-user-2011.html

Here's their official company page for their RevoScaleR package:

http://www.revolutionanalytics.com/products/enterprise-big-data.php

Basically this company is trying to establish themselves as kind of
the "Red Hat" of R -- providing support & commercial products to get R
more into the big commercial markets that have been dominated by SAS
for so long. The point is that they are very invested in working with
large data sets, and they have some heavy hitters in their company
(founder of SPSS, one of the R Core members, etc.), so I think their
products are probably worth a try.  The good news is that they offer a
free license of their otherwise expensive product to academics.

Here's another link to one of the Task Views on CRAN (which are
super-handy for finding good packages, if you've never looked at
them).  Scroll down to the bottom to find a "Large memory" etc.
heading, which refers to some packages that may be helpful.

On the other end of the complexity spectrum, the more primitive scan()
function sometimes works better for larger datasets than the
higher-level read.table() family of functions.

Finally, if all else fails, there was a post on the R forums a few
years ago that basically said the best solution for the memory problem
was to run the 64-bit Linux version of R with as much RAM as you could
cram onto the machine. If that's an option for you, it could be worth
a try as well.

good luck!
-scott
